guide.title: Bronx Park, the Bronx: A Garden and a Zoo in One Park
guide.intro: Bronx Park covers 718 acres, the eighth-largest park in New York City, bounded by Southern Boulevard, Webster Avenue, Gun Hill Road, Bronx Park East and East 180th Street. Much of the land came to the city under the 1884 New Parks Act, from Fordham University and from the Lorillard family, who had operated a snuff mill on the estate. Fordham Road divides the park between its two institutions: the New York Botanical Garden, founded in 1891, holds the northern 250 acres, and the Bronx Zoo, which opened on November 8, 1899, holds the southern 265. The Bronx River runs 2 miles through the park. Pelham Parkway adjoins it to the east, West Farms to the south and Belmont to the west.

sections.heading: A park, a garden and a zoo
sections.body:
Much of Bronx Park came to the city under the 1884 New Parks Act, from Fordham University and from the Lorillard family, who had operated a snuff mill beside the Bronx River. Fordham's Rose Hill campus spanned over 100 acres before that transfer reduced it, and the campus now stands immediately west of the Bronx Zoo and the New York Botanical Garden; a 138-plot cemetery on the campus was relocated in 1890 from its original location at what is now the Garden.

The river is the park's spine. It runs 2 miles (3.2 km) through Bronx Park, on a course of roughly 24 miles (39 km) from Westchester County to the East River that also carries it through the Garden and the Zoo. Lake Agassiz and Bronx Lake lie inside the park, along with waterfalls and ponds, and a 35-acre "Forever Wild" nature preserve occupies part of the northern section.

Fordham Road divides Bronx Park between its two institutions, and both the Bronx Zoo and the New York Botanical Garden stand at the road's eastern terminus in the park. The Garden was founded on April 28, 1891 by an act of the New York State Legislature and holds the northern 250 acres. Cornelius Vanderbilt II, Andrew Carnegie and J. P. Morgan were among its principal officers; Nathaniel Lord Britton served as secretary and led the fundraising campaign with his wife, Elizabeth Gertrude Britton, taking the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew in London as the model. The Bronx Zoo holds 265 acres in the southern section and opened on November 8, 1899, four years after members of the Boone and Crockett Club — principally Madison Grant and C. Grant LaFarge — founded the New York Zoological Society. William Temple Hornaday was its first director, and served thirty years.

One older building on the Garden's grounds predates both institutions. The Lorillard Snuff Mill, built around 1840 on Snuff Mill Road, was designated a New York City Landmark in 1966, before any designation the Garden or the Zoo carries, and became a National Historic Landmark in 1977.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Routes here run to a named gate rather than to the park as a whole, so which entrance you want decides which one to take.

By subway, the B, D and 4 stop at Bedford Park Boulevard; from there the Bx25 and Bx26 run east to the Botanical Garden's Mosholu Entrance, which is also reached on foot down Bedford Park Boulevard to Southern Boulevard. The 2 stops at Allerton Avenue for the Garden's East Gate — west on Allerton, then south on Bronx Park East to Waring Avenue — and that gate is pedestrian and daytime access only. The 2 also stops at Pelham Parkway for the Zoo, whose Bronx River entrance, Gate B, is west of there on foot. The Zoo's own page adds the 2 or 5 to West Farms Square–East Tremont, East 180th Street or Pelham Parkway without naming a gate for any of the three, so none of those is tied to an entrance here.

Metro-North's Harlem Line has a station named Botanical Garden, which serves the Garden's Mosholu Entrance.

Buses run to specific entrances too. The Bx19, Bx12, Bx22, Bx9 and Bx17 serve the Garden's Main Entrance at 2900 Southern Boulevard, and the Bx25, Bx26, Bx41 and Bx34 the Mosholu Entrance at 2950 Southern Boulevard. At the Zoo, the Bx9 and Bx19 stop at 183rd Street and Southern Boulevard for the Southern Boulevard pedestrian entrance, Gate C, as do the Bx12 and Bx22 at Fordham Road and Southern Boulevard, south on foot to the same gate. The Q44 from Queens stops at 180th Street and Boston Road, north on foot to the Asia entrance, Gate A. The BxM11 express, which stops along Madison Avenue between 26th and 99th Streets in Manhattan, runs direct to Gate B.

Neither institution's own directions page names an NYC Ferry landing.

The Garden's remaining gates are the Main Entrance, which takes vehicles and buses, and the Everett Garden Gate on Southern Boulevard at Fordham, for school groups only. The Zoo has a car-service drop-off at the Southern Boulevard gate, at Southern Boulevard and 185th Street.

faq.question: How do I get to Bronx Park?
faq.answer: By subway, the B, D and 4 stop at Bedford Park Boulevard for the Botanical Garden's Mosholu Entrance, and the 2 at Allerton Avenue for the Garden's East Gate or at Pelham Parkway for the Zoo's Bronx River entrance, Gate B. Metro-North's Harlem Line has a station named Botanical Garden, which serves the Mosholu Entrance. Buses run to particular gates rather than to the park as a whole, and the Getting there section lists which route serves which entrance.

faq.question: Why are the Botanical Garden and the Zoo in the same park?
faq.answer: Much of Bronx Park's land came to the city under the 1884 New Parks Act, from Fordham University and from the Lorillard family. The New York Botanical Garden was founded on April 28, 1891 by an act of the New York State Legislature and took 250 acres in the northern section; the Bronx Zoo opened on November 8, 1899 with 843 animals in 22 exhibits and holds 265 acres in the southern. Fordham Road divides the park between them, and both stand at the road's eastern terminus in Bronx Park. The Bronx River runs through both.

faq.question: What is the Lorillard Snuff Mill?
faq.answer: A stone mill built around 1840 by the P. Lorillard Company beside the Bronx River, of locally quarried schist, on what is now the New York Botanical Garden's grounds. The firm had moved its operations to the Bronx site in 1792 and abandoned the mill in 1870 for Jersey City. It was designated a New York City Landmark on April 19, 1966 and a National Historic Landmark on December 22, 1977. A $10.5 million restoration was completed in 2010, and it is now the Lillian and Amy Goldman Stone Mill, holding Garden staff offices and a catering facility rather than a public exhibit.

Lake Agassiz and Bronx Lake lie within the park, along with waterfalls and ponds, and a 35-acre "Forever Wild" nature preserve occupies part of the northern section. Adjacent neighborhoods are Pelham Parkway to the east, West Farms to the south and Belmont to the west.

places.name: New York Botanical Garden
places.address: Southern Boulevard and Bedford Park Boulevard, Bronx, NY
places.summary: A 250-acre botanical garden founded on April 28, 1891 by an act of the New York State Legislature, occupying the section of Bronx Park north of Fordham Road. It was designated a National Historic Landmark on May 28, 1967 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places the same day, reference number 67000009. Over a million people visit annually, on a 2016 figure that counts nearly 90,000 children from underserved communities and 3,000 teachers from New York City public schools.
places.history:
Cornelius Vanderbilt II, Andrew Carnegie and J. P. Morgan were among the Garden's principal officers. Nathaniel Lord Britton served as secretary and led the fundraising campaign with his wife, Elizabeth Gertrude Britton, taking the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew in London as the model.

Ground was broken for the Enid A. Haupt Conservatory on January 3, 1899 and it was completed in 1902 at a cost of $177,000, built by John R. Sheehan for the city's Department of Parks and Recreation. Lord & Burnham designed it, with William R. Cobb as primary designer, in an Italian Renaissance style modelled on Kew's Palm House and Joseph Paxton's Crystal Palace: a 512-foot "C" of eleven pavilions under a 90-foot central dome. Renovations in 1935 and 1950 removed the original decoration, and a 1978 restoration led by Edward Larrabee Barnes moved the building back toward it, funded by Enid Annenberg Haupt's $5 million gift and a $5 million maintenance endowment; it was renamed for her that year. Beyer Blinder Belle carried out a $25 million renovation between 1993 and 1997. The Conservatory was designated a New York City landmark on October 16, 1973, the date the Landmarks Preservation Commission's designation report carries.

The LuEsther T. Mertz Library was founded in 1899, in a Renaissance Revival building designed by Robert W. Gibson and completed in 1900. It was first the Museum Building, then the Administration Building, and was renamed for its donor in the 1990s. It became a National Historic Landmark contributing property on May 28, 1967 and a New York City landmark on March 24, 2009. Its holdings include two copies of the Circa Instans, of about 1190 and about 1275, and a 2002 New York Times article stated that the collection held "75 percent of all systematic botany literature in the world and 70 percent of all flora that had been published." The William & Lynda Steere Herbarium, founded in 1891 and housed in the Garden's International Plant Science Center, holds roughly 7.2 to 7.8 million specimens, among them the Columbia College herbarium acquired in 1895 with some 600,000 specimens.

The Thain Family Forest covers 50 acres along the Bronx River, old growth tracing to pre-colonial Lenapehoking. Eastern hemlock was historically dominant in a canopy of oak, beech and sweet gum, and declined in the early twentieth century under hemlock woolly adelgid and elongate hemlock scale infestation. It was called Hemlock Grove first and Native Forest for a time before taking its present name. Britton called the site "the most precious natural possession of the city of New York," and the Garden's site was chosen in 1895 primarily for this forest; John and Carmen Thain supported a 2011 restoration that removed invasive species and expanded native vegetation.

Beatrix Jones Farrand designed the rose garden in 1916 and it was renovated in 2007. Charles Tefft sculpted the Fountain of Life in 1905. The Everett Children's Garden opened in 1998, the International Plant Science Center in 2002, the Leon Levy Visitor Center in 2004, the Pfizer Plant Research Laboratory in 2006, the Hudson Garden Grill in 2015 and the Edible Academy in 2018.

photos.title: Enid A. Haupt Conservatory
photos.description: The main glasshouse dome of the Enid A. Haupt Conservatory at the New York Botanical Garden, seen looking west on a hazy midday, with the glazed rotunda rising above the surrounding trees.
photos.author: Jim.henderson

places.name: Bronx Zoo
places.summary: A 265-acre zoo in the section of Bronx Park south of Fordham Road, which opened on November 8, 1899 with 843 animals in 22 exhibits. It is managed by the Wildlife Conservation Society, founded in 1895 as the New York Zoological Society, and is accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums.
places.history:
Members of the Boone and Crockett Club — principally Madison Grant and C. Grant LaFarge — founded the New York Zoological Society in 1895, four years before the zoo opened. William Temple Hornaday served as its first director for thirty years. As of 2010 the collection held about 4,000 animals of 650 species, and the zoo recorded 2.1 million average yearly visitors as of 2009.

Heins & LaFarge designed the original permanent buildings as Beaux-Arts pavilions around a circular sea lion pool. That group, Astor Court, was designated a New York City landmark on June 20, 2000, an attempt in 1966 having failed. Paul Manship's Rainey Memorial Gates, dedicated in 1934 as a memorial to the big-game hunter Paul James Rainey, were designated a New York City landmark on January 11, 1967 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972. The Rockefeller Fountain was designated on February 20, 1968, and the Zoo Center — built in 1908 in Beaux-Arts style as the Elephant House — was landmarked in 2000.

The American Bison Society was founded in 1905, and in 1913 fourteen bison were sent from the zoo to Montana's National Bison Range and to Wind Cave National Park. The zoo was the first in the United States to exhibit shoebills and Komodo dragons, both in 1926, and the first in North America to exhibit an okapi, in 1937. It held four thylacines between 1902 and 1919; the last died on September 13, 1919.

Congo Gorilla Forest opened in 1999 over 6.5 acres, with a visitor trail about a third of a mile long and some 400 plant species, and had taken 7 million visits by 2009. Western lowland gorillas share it with okapis, red river hogs, mandrills, Congo peafowl, African pygmy geese, western long-tailed hornbills, fire skinks and Nile monitors; it is open March through December, with indoor viewing when the weather is colder. JungleWorld shows the jungles of Asia, its residents including white-cheeked gibbon, Indian gharial, tapir, Asian small-clawed otters, Rodrigues fruit bats and silver leaf langur, and the Wildlife Conservation Society works with the Madras Crocodile Bank Trust Center for Herpetology on gharial conservation connected to it.

Himalayan Highlands opened on June 27, 1986. The Gelada Reserve, originally the Baboon Reserve, opened in 1990 and won an Association of Zoos and Aquariums exhibit award in 1991; Tiger Mountain opened on May 15, 2003 and won one in 2004. Madagascar! opened on June 20, 2008 in the former Lion House, which had opened in 1903. World of Darkness, which the zoo's own account calls the world's first major exhibit designed specifically for nocturnal animals, opened in 1969, closed in 2009 amid budget cuts and reopened on July 12, 2025.

places.name: Lorillard Snuff Mill
places.address: Snuff Mill Road, New York Botanical Garden, Bronx, NY
places.summary: A stone mill built around 1840 by the P. Lorillard Company beside the Bronx River, of locally quarried schist, standing on Snuff Mill Road within the New York Botanical Garden's grounds. Its own Wikipedia article calls it the oldest existing tobacco manufacturing building in the United States. It is now the Lillian and Amy Goldman Stone Mill and holds Garden staff offices and a catering facility.
places.history: The Lorillard firm had moved its operations to this Bronx site in 1792 and abandoned the mill in 1870, when it went to Jersey City. The building was designated a New York City Landmark on April 19, 1966, then a National Historic Landmark and listed on the National Register of Historic Places on December 22, 1977, reference number 77000935, and entered on the New York State Register on June 23, 1980. A renovation in 1952–54 added a café, a patio and a meeting room, and a $10.5 million restoration was completed in 2010.

photos.title: Lorillard Snuff Mill above the Bronx River
photos.description: The stone mill building on the left bank of the Bronx River, looking north on a hazy midday, with the water in the foreground and trees framing the mill.
photos.author: Jim.henderson

places.name: Bronx River Forest
places.summary: A wooded area along the Bronx River corridor whose southern extent reaches into the New York Botanical Garden. The Bronx River Alliance describes it as a remnant of the original forests and floodplains that once blanketed the Bronx River corridor, and records many trees exceeding 100 years in age. Upgraded paths, nature trails, boardwalks and overlooks run through it.
places.history: The Bronx River Alliance manages the forest in partnership with the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation and, by the Alliance's own account, more than a hundred partner organizations. Recent work has focused on floodplain restoration, habitat expansion and public-access infrastructure.
